All of these technologies have strengths and weaknesses to reach the goal of deploying a monitoring system in debris dense regions. There is a so called "mm-size gap" where currently no dedicated measurements of the space debris population exist, but the energy upon impact with these particles can still be mission critical. It is thus required to bring down the uncertainties in this size regime. Mission proposals are being studied to close the gap, or at least demonstrate the capability of characterising the population. Promising technologies are non-destructive measurements if they succeed in creating large effective detection areas. However, precursor studies are ongoing and parallel developments have not been systematically compared and trade-off yet.This activity encompasses the following tasks: - Compare and assess the three technologies, and where possible COTS versions, w.r.t. the objective of providing a long-term monitoring capability at orbital altitudes of 800 and 500km. - Optimise detector design with regards to minimal complexity/risk/cost and maximal number of detectable particles in the mm range. - Breadboard the critical detector technologies.
